gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own AC180 page pairs the 1,152 Wh AC180 with its B80 (806 Wh), B230 (2,048 Wh) or B300 (3,072 Wh) battery packs, 'for a total of up to 4,224Wh', and says the AC180's 2,700 W Power Lifting Mode is meant for resistive heaters.
standout_why: I opened three of the cited rival pages on 2026-11-14. Volt & Valley lists the AC180 at 1,800 W and about 39 min but says nothing about expansion batteries or Power Lifting. It covers expansion only for the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max and Anker SOLIX F3800, and it names SurgePad and X-Boost without explaining either. UTrendCo lists the AC180 at about 39 min and says nothing about expansion or boost modes. Lights On Lab gives 1.3 h on low for the AC180 and also says nothing about expansion or modes. I could not read the cited Tested Watts page: WebFetch failed on a certificate error, and my curl fallback needed an approval it didn't get. So I can't rule out that Tested Watts covers this. Our own current page doesn't have it either.
decides: It strengthens the case for the BLUETTI AC180 (which Dealectric lists under awin:bluetti_us) as the roughly 1 kWh pick for someone who wants to run a heater. It is the only one of our listed roughly 1 kWh units with a maker-sourced add-on battery path. That path takes it from about 39 min to about 2.4 h of runtime by the arithmetic with a B300 (4,224 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,500 W = 2.39 h), with a caveat on how the packs feed power, explained in the notes. Power Lifting itself doesn't change the answer for a 1,500 W heater, because the AC180's 1,800 W rated output already covers it. I could not source expansion support for the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 or the EcoFlow DELTA 3 / 3 Plus from maker pages, so the page must not claim they can't expand.

findings.label: AC rated output
findings.value: 1,800 W total from 120 V / 15 A outlets; 2,700 W surge
findings.note: 1,800 W rated is 300 W above a 1,500 W heater's draw.

findings.label: Power Lifting Mode
findings.value: boosts output to 2,700 W; maker says it is 'ideal for pure-resistive heating devices like hair dryers, electric kettles, and heaters'
findings.note: The footnote doesn't say whether output voltage is lowered in this mode. A 1,500 W heater fits inside the normal 1,800 W rating, so the mode isn't needed for this question. It would only matter for a heater rated above 1,800 W.

findings.label: Maker-stated battery pairings
findings.value: B80 (806 Wh), B230 (2,048 Wh) or B300 (3,072 Wh); 'for a total of up to 4,224Wh'
findings.note: Arithmetic: 1,152 + 3,072 = 4,224 Wh, matching the maker's total. Heater on high: 4,224 × 0.85 ÷ 1,500 = 2.39 h (about 2 h 24 min). With B230: 3,200 × 0.85 ÷ 1,500 = 1.81 h. With B80: 1,958 × 0.85 ÷ 1,500 = 1.11 h. Caveat: the page says how much capacity these packs add but not how they connect or at what rate they feed the AC180. If they feed through a charging input slower than 1,500 W, a heater on high would drain the AC180's internal battery first, and the full combined runtime might not be reachable at 1,500 W. Confirm in the AC180 manual before printing these runtimes.

findings.label: Rival coverage of expansion and boost modes
findings.value: Volt & Valley mentions expansion only for the DELTA 2 Max (2 to 6 kWh) and F3800 (to 53.8 kWh), and X-Boost only as '3,400W available' for the DELTA 2 Max; UTrendCo and Lights On Lab mention neither
findings.source_title: What Size Power Station to Run a Space Heater? The Real Math | Volt & Valley
findings.note: Also checked https://utrendco.com/blog/can-portable-power-station-run-space-heater and https://www.lightsonlab.com/blog/can-a-power-station-run-a-space-heater/ on 2026-11-14. Neither covers expansion batteries, X-Boost, Power Lifting or SurgePad.
